metaDescription: Push lawn mowers compared across reel, corded, cordless and gas designs, with cut quality, weight, runtime and lawn-size fit explained plainly.
expertTake: The Greenworks 40V 16-inch is the best push mower for most small lawns because it is light, quiet and starts with a button, the Scotts 20-inch reel is the value pick for a fine-turf lawn, and the SENIX 21-inch gas push is the one for rougher ground. Skip push mowers entirely if your lawn is large or sloped: you will want drive assist.
introParagraphs: A push mower relies on you for the one thing that costs the most effort: forward motion. That makes weight, wheel size and handle geometry matter as much as the cutting system, because you carry the machine across the lawn on every pass. The category also spans very different cutting technologies, from a scissor-action reel to a spinning blade.

Choosing well means matching the cutting method to your grass and the power source to your patience. Reel designs are quiet and gentle but demand frequent mowing, cordless units trade runtime for convenience and gas units trade weight and maintenance for stamina. This guide compares each approach on the practical numbers that decide a weekly mow.

products.name: Greenworks 40V 16-Inch Cordless Push
products.description:
Greenworks uses a lightweight deck that the listing says is 35 percent lighter than steel, paired with a 40-volt battery that claims up to a third of an acre per charge in ideal conditions. The practical benefit is that a light deck is easier to push, turn and lift, which matters more than motor power on a small lawn.

Push-button start means no pull cord and no fuel mixing. Five height positions cover typical cool and warm season settings. The 16-inch width is narrow, so it makes more passes than a 21-inch gas mower on the same lawn.

Running time drops in thick or wet grass, and the claim is for light, dry conditions. Keep the battery indoors, charge before long mows and clean the deck underside. Against the WORX it offers a simpler single-battery setup but a smaller deck. Hose the deck off gently and never aim a pressure washer at the motor housing.
products.bestFor: Small lawns up to roughly a quarter acre where light weight and quiet matter.
pros: Light deck is easy to push and lift
Single battery is simple to charge
cons: Runtime shrinks in thick or wet grass

products.name: WORX WG745 40V 17-Inch Brushless 2-in-1
products.description:
WORX uses two 20-volt, 4.0Ah batteries combined for 40 volts, which means the same packs can run other 20V WORX tools. The brushless motor claims higher cutting power and efficiency than earlier designs, and the 17-inch deck is a step wider than Greenworks.

A 2-in-1 deck mulches or bags to the rear, but has no side discharge. Mulching suits frequent mowing, and bagging suits leaves and seed heads. The listing positions it for a quarter acre.

The trade is a slightly heavier machine with two batteries to charge. Compared with the Greenworks 16-inch it covers more per pass and shares batteries with a wider tool family. A spare pair of batteries doubles the area you can cover on a big weekend.
products.bestFor: Quarter acre lawns for owners of WORX 20V tools.
pros: 20V batteries share with other WORX tools
cons: Two batteries to charge and store

products.name: Scotts 2000-20S 20-Inch 5-Blade Reel
products.description:
A reel mower cuts like scissors: spinning blades pass a fixed bedknife and shear the grass cleanly. The Scotts 20-inch uses five heat-treated alloy steel blades on ball bearings and a quick-snap height range of 1 to 3 inches.

That clean cut is healthier for turf than the tearing of a dull rotary blade, and there is no fuel, battery or cord. It is also quiet, and the wheels turn the blades, so the faster you walk the better it cuts.

Reels demand frequent mowing, and they struggle with tall grass, twigs and weeds. They also need the bedknife aligned. For a small, well-kept lawn, it is the lowest-cost, lowest-maintenance option here. Mow when the grass is dry, since wet clippings gum up a reel.
products.bestFor: Small, level, well-kept lawns of fine grass.
pros: Scissor cut is healthier for grass
cons: Struggles with tall grass and weeds

products.name: American Lawn Mower 1204-14 14-Inch 4-Blade Reel
products.description:
This 14-inch reel is the narrowest mower here, with four blades and 8.5-inch polymer wheels. The adjustable height range of 0.5 to 1.75 inches is low, suited to bermuda, zoysia and other fine, low-cut turf.

Its maker states that it can handle grass up to 4 inches tall, but the practical advice is to mow before the grass gets that high. The narrow width fits tight spaces and the light frame is easy to store.

Compared with the Scotts 20-inch it covers less per pass but is lighter and cheaper. Keep the bedknife adjusted and the blades clean. Because it is so light, it is also the easiest mower here to store in a shed corner.
products.bestFor: Tiny lawns and fine turf kept low.
pros: Very light and easy to store

products.name: LawnMaster LMRM1801 18-Inch 5-Blade Reel
products.description:
LawnMaster adds nine height positions and 10-inch front wheels to an 18-inch five-blade reel. A scissor-like cut avoids ripping or tearing of grass blades, and the wider height range lets you adapt across seasons.

Large front wheels make it easier to pivot and roll over small bumps. Against the Scotts, it is a little narrower but offers finer height control.

As with all reels, it works best on small lawns mown often. Adjust the reel-to-bedknife contact before the season and keep it sharp. Set the reel contact with a strip of newspaper: it should snip cleanly.
products.bestFor: Small lawns where height flexibility matters.
pros: Scissor cut is gentle on grass
cons: 18-inch deck is slow on bigger lawns

products.name: LawnMaster MEB1114K 15-Inch 11A Corded Electric
products.description:
A corded electric mower has unlimited runtime, no battery cost and a push-button start. The 11-amp motor spins the blade at 3,300 rpm under a 14-inch cutting width, with five height positions.

The cord is the limitation. You need a heavy outdoor extension cord, you must manage it around trees and beds, and you can mow only as far as the cord reaches. On a small, simple lawn near an outlet it is the cheapest powered option.

Compared with the Greenworks, it never runs out of power but cuts less per pass and gets tangled. Store the cord neatly and inspect it for nicks. Always mow away from the cord, keeping it on the cut side of the lawn.
products.bestFor: Very small, simple lawns near an outdoor outlet.
cons: Cord limits reach and can tangle
Cord must be watched for damage

products.name: SENIX 21-Inch 144cc Gas Push 3-in-1
products.description:
SENIX is the conventional gas push mower: a 144cc four-stroke engine under a 21-inch steel deck that can mulch, bag or discharge to the side. It handles thick, wet or overgrown grass better than any electric or reel machine here.

The price is weight, noise and upkeep. You push all of it, you change the oil and you manage fuel. On a lawn of a third of an acre or more, it is the machine that will not run out of runtime.

Compared with the cordless units it is heavier but cuts a wider path. A sharp blade and fresh fuel matter more than anything else. Drain or stabilize fuel before storing it for the winter.
products.bestFor: Larger flat lawns and rough grass that cordless units struggle with.
cons: Loud with fuel and oil upkeep

buyingCriteria.explanation: A reel, like the Scotts 20-inch, shears grass like scissors and suits short, fine turf mown often. A rotary blade, as in the Greenworks, WORX and SENIX, tears slightly but handles taller, thicker grass. Pick based on your grass type and how often you will mow. A quick test is whether your grass is under three inches at every mow; if yes, a reel is a real option.

A push mower's weight is your effort. The Greenworks claims a deck 35 percent lighter than steel, and the reels are lighter still, while a gas SENIX is the heaviest. Try lifting the mower, since you may need to lift it into a car or up steps. Add the weight of a full battery or a gallon of fuel when comparing machines.

A 14-inch reel like the American Lawn Mower takes many passes, while a 21-inch deck covers about 50 percent more per pass. Match width to lawn size: small yards suit 14 to 17 inches, larger yards suit 20 inches and up.

Cordless units like the WORX WG745 have limited runtime but start with a button. Corded units like the LawnMaster MEB1114K never run down but need a cord. Gas units run as long as you have fuel but need upkeep. Check whether a spare battery is sold separately, because it is the easiest way to extend runtime.
The American Lawn Mower reel goes as low as 0.5 inch, suited to fine turf, while the LawnMaster reel offers nine positions. A wide range lets you raise the cut in summer.

A 2-in-1 or 3-in-1 deck, like the WORX and SENIX, gives you options. Reel mowers usually do neither well, leaving short clippings to fall. Check whether you prefer mulching or bagging. Mulching only works if the clippings are short, so mow often when you choose it.

specDecoder.meaning: A spinning cylinder of curved blades that shear grass against a bedknife. More blades give a finer cut. Reels need the blades to touch the bedknife lightly, so set them each spring.
specDecoder.watchFor: Scotts and LawnMaster have 5 blades; American Lawn Mower has 4.

specDecoder.meaning: A motor without carbon brushes, running cooler and more efficiently. It stretches battery runtime.
Battery capacity. Multiply by volts for watt-hours to compare runtime. Watt-hours equal volts times amp-hours.
Motor current. A higher amp rating usually means more cutting power.
Displacement. More cc usually means more torque in thick grass.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cut quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the cutting methods, giving reels credit for scissor action and rotary decks credit for tall-grass capability. The Scotts and LawnMaster reels scored highest on cut quality.

howWeEvaluated.title: Weight and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at deck material, wheel size and handle design. The Greenworks lightweight deck and the LawnMaster 10-inch front wheels earned the most credit. We gave extra weight to wheel size, since big wheels cut pushing effort on uneven lawns.

howWeEvaluated.title: Power source practicality
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed battery runtime, cord reach and fuel upkeep. Owner feedback patterns on thin runtime claims shaped the scoring.

howWeEvaluated.title: Width and height range
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared deck width from 14 to 21 inches and height range from 0.5 to 3.75 inches. Narrow decks were not penalized when the machine suits the lawn it is sold for.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated the Scotts as the value pick from the Greenworks as the overall pick, matching each machine to the lawn size it suits.

cards.label: Reel
cards.text: The Scotts, LawnMaster and American Lawn Mower reels cut like scissors, are silent and need no fuel. They need frequent mowing and struggle with weeds.

cards.label: Rotary
cards.text: The Greenworks, WORX and SENIX use a spinning blade that handles tall grass and mulches. They tear slightly and need power.

howToChoose.note: Pick reel for fine, well-kept turf, rotary for ordinary or rough lawns.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for light weight, easy storage and a narrow deck. A small lawn rewards simplicity over capacity.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The American Lawn Mower 14-inch reel is the lightest, and the Greenworks 16-inch is the lightest powered option.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: Spend more if you mow weekly and value quiet starts and low upkeep, which points to the Greenworks or WORX.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Save if the lawn is small and level. A reel such as the Scotts costs little and needs almost no care.

maintenance.why: A dull blade tears grass. Reels need bedknife adjustment as well.
Wet clippings cake and rot the deck. Disconnect power first.
Keep lithium packs at partial charge in a cool place.
Fresh oil protects the engine under load.
A nicked cord is a shock hazard.

faq.a: On small, level lawns of fine grass, yes. They give a clean cut, are silent and need no fuel. They struggle with tall grass and weeds.

faq.q: How long will a cordless push mower run?
faq.a: Claims like a third of an acre per charge assume light, dry grass. Expect less in thick or wet conditions.

faq.q: Is gas still worth it for a push mower?
faq.a: For larger or rough lawns, yes. Gas has no runtime limit and handles wet grass, at the cost of weight and upkeep.

faq.q: Do corded mowers need special cords?
faq.a: Yes. Use an outdoor-rated heavy-gauge extension cord and keep it behind you.

faq.q: What height should I mow at?
faq.a: Most lawns do well at 2.5 to 3.5 inches, never removing more than a third of the blade at once.

faq.q: How often should I sharpen the blade?
faq.a: Once or twice a season. A dull blade shreds grass tips and browns the lawn.
